JD Vance hasn’t even said he’s running in 2028, and his own party is already running a soft launch of “Never Vance.”

The attacks brand him “unfit,” accuse him — without evidence — of freelancing foreign policy behind Trump’s back, and compare him to Obama and Bernie Sanders. Allies say the timing is the tell: two years before the primary, with Vance still the polling front‑runner and Rubio slowly gaining ground as the business‑friendly alternative.

Vance’s camp is leaning into the backlash. The vice president himself has gone full anti‑influence narrative, citing a Time report on a pro‑Israel operation run by a former Trump digital aide and telling Rogan his answer to paid smears is “go to hell, I represent Americans first.”

Underneath the memes and “Never Vance” slogans is a serious question: who owns the post‑Trump GOP’s foreign policy — the war‑skeptical populist vice president, or the donors and media figures who still want the party to sound like 2004 on Israel and Iran? The knives are out because everyone knows the answer will decide more than just one primary.

🏗 Tokenization can make finance faster. It does not make risk disappear.

On a shared digital ledger, processes that traditionally happen one after another can happen almost simultaneously:

• execution
• clearing
• settlement
• transfer of ownership

That can reduce delays and remove some operational friction.

But it also changes where failure can occur.

The important questions become:

• Who operates the infrastructure?
• Where is the authoritative ownership record?
• What happens during an outage?
• Who can correct an incorrect transaction?
• Who absorbs the loss when software and legal records disagree?

An IMF analysis warns that tokenization may move risk away from traditional financial institutions and toward the companies operating digital ledgers, wallets and market infrastructure.

The rail becomes faster.

The responsibility still needs an owner.

Technology changes the process.
Architecture decides where the risk goes.

Source: IMF, Tokenization Can Change the World’s Financial Architecture
